messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi had always thought of himself as steady and practical, the kind of man who could wire a house in the dark if he had to, but that confidence changed after the night he was mugged on his way home from work. He had been walking from the bus stop through a narrow side street, carrying his tools, when two men came close too quickly, one of them moving with a sudden lurch that made Ravi freeze before he understood what was happening. The men crowded him against a wall, one reeking of alcohol, and in the roughness of their hands and the speed of their movements he felt entirely trapped. They took his wallet and left him shaken and humiliated, standing alone under a streetlight with his heart pounding long after they were gone.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi began to wake from nightmares with the same jolt that had greeted him that night, his body already braced before he was fully awake. Those mornings left him unsettled for hours, as if the fear from sleep had spilled into the day and made him wary of everything around him. He had come to believe that the world was most dangerous when he was not prepared, and that feeling lingered especially at night, when the streets were quiet and he could not trust what might be hiding in the dark. Crowded places made that sense of danger sharper still; if people pressed too close in a shop or on the sidewalk, he found himself scanning faces and exits, certain that strangers approaching him could mean trouble even in ordinary situations. What frightened him most was not only the memory of being robbed, but the way these moments seemed to bring the threat back so vividly that he felt on guard again before anything had happened.

As a result, Ravi began arranging his days around those moments of alarm. He avoided going out after sunset unless he absolutely had to, and he became tense whenever he passed through busy markets or stopped at the depot where men gathered near the entrance. In his work as an electrician, he had once been comfortable moving between homes and construction sites, chatting easily with clients and neighbors, but now he was more guarded when a customer opened the door too quickly or when someone crossed the room behind him without warning. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard, and he often caught himself stepping back, watching hands and shoulders instead of listening to what was being said. He noticed alcohol smell in particular at gas stations and in the hallways of apartment buildings where he worked, and it brought back the ugliness of that alley with such force that his chest tightened and he wanted to leave at once.

Over time, Ravi’s sense of safety narrowed. At night he checked the locks more than once and kept the hallway light on longer than his wife preferred, saying little about why he stayed awake listening for footsteps. During the day he could still function, but he did so with a constant readiness, as if he had to be prepared for a stranger to close in or for a sudden movement to turn into danger. That vigilance wore on him and made him less willing to take jobs in unfamiliar parts of town, which strained his routine and left him embarrassed about seeming frailer than he felt inside. He was careful not to mention the robbery too often, telling himself that dwelling on it would only make him weaker, yet the fear kept returning in the same places: after a nightmare, in a crowd, when he caught the smell of alcohol, or when someone moved too fast nearby. Each of those moments seemed to confirm that he still was not safe.

By the time he finally sought help, Ravi had become troubled by how much of his life was being organized around staying protected. His wife had noticed that he looked worn down after poor sleep and that he no longer wanted to accompany her to evening gatherings or crowded community events. What brought him in was the realization that even ordinary encounters with strangers were now making him feel threatened, and he no longer trusted his own ability to settle after a nightmare or relax at night. He came hoping to feel safe again in the dark, to stop bracing at every sudden movement, and to reclaim some ordinary freedom in the streets and homes where he still needed to work.
